title: Derivative-free bound-constrained optimization for solving structured problems with surrogate models
contribution: A model-based trust-region DFO framework for box-constrained composite problems h(F(x)) that may use surrogate or history-based regression values at interpolation points, with accuracy tied to the trust-region radius, a bound-respecting interpolation-set routine and a convergence proof (arXiv v3 pp. 2, 11-13, 17-21).
problem_entry: Black-box evaluations are the bottleneck; existing model-based DFO methods never use cheap approximate values at interpolation points, although surrogates or evaluations from related, previously solved instances exist (pp. 1-2, 5-7).
key_idea: Keep the standard fully-linear trust-region DFO framework and let interpolation values be approximations with error at most kappa_app*delta_k, delta_k = c_app*Delta_k^2, while iterates and trial points are still evaluated exactly (pp. 4, 11-12).
assumptions: Fi C1 with Lipschitz values/gradients, h C2 Lipschitz with bounded derivatives, f bounded below, noise-free sure accuracy, unrelaxable box; fully linear models every iteration assumed for simplicity (Remark 1) (pp. 7-9, 12-13, 19).
proof_devices: Fully linear models from approximate interpolation values, adapting Wild's Theorem 4.1 with an extra kappa_app*Delta^2 term (Lemma 2.4, p. 10; pp. 29-30)
Standard trust-region DFO lemma chain B.1-B.7 to lim pi_k^f = 0 (Theorem 2.8, p. 13; pp. 33-37)
Explicit well-poisedness threshold xi for +/- null-space directions projected onto the box (Lemmas 3.1-3.4, Theorem 3.5, pp. 15-17)
Projection test equals the last pivot of a QR factorization (Lemma 3.6, p. 18)
Regression error bound via translation invariance and affine weights beta^T 1 = 1, then ||beta||_1 bound through sigma_min (Lemmas 4.2-4.3, Theorem 4.4, pp. 20-21)
experiments: Python implementation; AlgH vs in-framework ablation Alg-empty (no history) on the COPS methanol-to-hydrocarbons least-squares problem, T = 100 related instances, budget 2p(nx+1) = 252 evaluations, 100 macro replications with a 1.96 sigma/sqrt(N) band; other problems tested but not shown; no external DFO code run (pp. 22-25).
positioning: Extends the convex-constrained trust-region DFO frameworks of Hough-Roberts [26] and Conejo et al. [10] and the structure-exploiting least-squares line (DFO-GN, POUNDERS, DFLS); credits Conn-Vicente for prior-value reuse without a mechanism (pp. 6-7, 11-12).
writing: One 'distinguishing feature' sentence in abstract and conclusion; proofs moved to a supplement 'for completeness'; claim wording ('outperforms a state-of-the-art DFO algorithm') outruns the in-framework ablation actually run (pp. 1-2, 13, 22, 24-25).
limits_future: Limits visible but uncollected: exact evaluations still needed at iterates/trial points, noise-free, fully linear models every iteration, box only, one problem shown; future: extension to closed convex sets conjectured (pp. 4, 7, 12, 23).

method_links.note: Accuracy of the cheap inner quantity (surrogate/regression value) is derived from what the trust-region globalization needs, delta_k = c_app*Delta_k^2, keeping fully linear models; inner object is a function-value surrogate, not a linear/QP solve.
Rival built inside the same framework with one component switched off (Alg-empty); 100 macro replications with confidence band.
No external code run although DFO-LS/POUNDERS discussed; one of several problems shown; abstract calls the in-framework ablation 'a state-of-the-art DFO algorithm'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: amortize evaluations across a sequence of related instances
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: History of black-box values from previously solved instances feeds a regression surrogate with a provable accuracy radius; gain grows with history size (over half the budget approximated by t ~ 10).

transferable: Tie the allowed error of cheap approximations to the square of the trust-region radius so fully linear theory applies unchanged (pp. 4, 11).
Bound a regression estimate's absolute error through affine weights (sum to one) and the l1 norm of the weight vector (pp. 20-21).
Replace a nonconvex geometry subproblem by +/- coordinate-direction projections onto the box and prove an explicit well-poisedness threshold (p. 17).
Identify a geometric well-poisedness test with a QR pivot so the code check and the proof quantity coincide (p. 18).
Plot the mechanism count (evaluations replaced by approximations) beside the cumulative-improvement curve with a confidence band over macro replications (p. 24).

quotes.text: The main difference between our algorithm and other modern model-based DFO frameworks is that function value approximations may be used at interpolation points in place of exact function values.
Importantly, the actual value of κapp need not be known by our algorithmic framework.

title: Incremental quasi-Newton algorithms for solving a nonconvex, nonsmooth, finite-sum optimization problem
contribution: Five incremental BFGS variants (direct, DC, smoothed, locally convexified, strongly convexified) for the nonsmooth nonconvex transductive SVM objective, tested on 12 data sets against a bundle method (arXiv v1 pp. 2, 10-19).
problem_entry: The TSVM objective is nonconvex and nonsmooth and the IQN/IBFGS method has guarantees only for convex smooth sums; the paper asks whether IQN strategies are nonetheless viable (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Keep the IBFGS skeleton and change only how the gradient displacement is formed (DC subgradient freeze, smoothing, weak-convexity shift 2*rho*s, regularizer redistribution) so curvature pairs stay positive and updates are not skipped (pp. 7, 10-13).
assumptions: None for the tested methods (guarantees 'elusive'); locally Lipschitz objective with Clarke generalized gradients; a cited local superlinear guarantee holds only for a fixed strongly convex, Lipschitz-Hessian approximation with cyclic order (pp. 2, 9, 13-15).
proof_devices: Weak convexity of the smoothed objective from convex Lipschitz outer composed with smooth inner, explicit rho_i >= 2(||x_i||^2+1)/mu blowing up as mu -> 0 (Proposition 2.4, pp. 6-7)
Strong convexity plus Lipschitz gradient gives two-sided curvature bounds (Lemma 2.5, p. 8)
Local superlinear convergence cited from Mokhtari et al. (Lemmas 3.2-3.3, Theorem 3.4, pp. 14-15)
experiments: 12 data sets, 10-100% labelled data, ten-fold CV on sets 1-8; baseline TSVM-Bundle with published parameters, same iteration limits and starts, Gurobi subproblems; average testing error table plus performance profile on a best-to-worst normalized objective measure; C1, C2 chosen by best testing-set results; timing only in passing (prototypes); runs per set not stated (pp. 15-19).
positioning: Builds on IQN of Mokhtari, Eisen and Ribeiro and on his own nonsmooth BFGS work (Curtis-Que; Curtis-Robinson-Zhou); novelty claimed narrowly as no prior work on these IBFGS variants (pp. 2-3, 21).
writing: Question-and-answer contribution paragraph ('Our answer is in the affirmative'); open about missing theory; per-variant motivation before pseudocode; a design caveat recorded; strong headline 'all outperform a state-of-the-art bundle method' (pp. 1-2, 10-13, 20).
limits_future: Stated: no guarantees, prototype codes so no detailed timing, smoothing-parameter mixing caveat; unstated: one formulation, test-set hyperparameter selection, profile measure differs from table measure; no future directions (pp. 2, 12, 15-16, 20).

method_links.note: External baseline given the same iteration limits, starting points and its published parameters; full per-instance table printed including rows where it wins.

C1, C2 selected by best testing-set results; timing compared only in passing against a Gurobi-backed code; number of random runs not stated; 'all outperform' not narrowed although Table 2 shows the bundle method best in many rows.
Conclusion rests on a performance profile over a normalized objective-value measure while the application's testing-error table is mixed; whether the measure favours I-BFGS is not asked.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: repair the curvature pair through problem structure
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Keep the quasi-Newton skeleton and modify only y (DC subgradient freeze, weak-convexity shift, strong-convexity redistribution) when the information model changes; close to Heuristic 10 at the level of the secant pair.

transferable: Freeze the concave part's subgradient in a DC split to guarantee s^T y >= 0 for a BFGS update (pp. 11-12).
Shift y by 2*rho*s using an explicit weak-convexity modulus of a smoothed component (pp. 7, 13).
Distribute a common regularizer across finite-sum components so each is strongly convex and component-wise assumptions hold (p. 7).
Compute the weak-convexity modulus of a smoothed term as a function of mu to see why the unsmoothed term cannot be convexified (pp. 6-7).
Print the full per-instance outcome table beside the summary profile so readers see where the incumbent wins (pp. 16-19).

quotes.text: Our main goal is to answer the question: Can IQN (such as IBFGS) strategies be effective and efficient when solving the nonconvex and nonsmooth problem (2)
Since ours are only prototype implementations of the methods, we do not provide detailed time comparisons of the runs.
